earlier_scan.note: Fixed rule: stress the vowel before the last consonant; suffix-conditioned antepenult exceptions (-le/-ne/-re, -ic, -ula etc.).

new_statements.quote: § 10. The main STRESS is normally on the vowel before the last consonant. The plural ending does not change the original stress of the word. Adjectives and nouns ending in -le, -ne, and -re preceded by a vowel have the stress on the third syllable from the end; e.g. fragile, ordine, tempore. In words formed with the suffixes -ic, -ica, -ico, -ide, -ido, -ula, and -ulo, the stress falls on the syllable preceding the suffix. The suffixes -ific and -ifico are stressed on the first i. [...] Note: Words without consonant or without a vowel before the last consonant are stressed of necessity on the first vowel; e.g. io, via, and certain present-tense forms, as strue, crea, etc.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: stress the syllable containing the last vowel that precedes the word's final consonant, i.e. the final syllable in consonant-final words (esser, parlar) and the penult in words ending in -CV (lingua, requirimento); plural -s/-es is ignored; words with no vowel before the last consonant (io, via, crea) take stress on the first vowel. Lexically/suffixally specified antepenults: -le/-ne/-re after a vowel (fragile, ordine, tempore), -ic(a/o), -ide/-ido, -ula/-ulo, -issim-, -esim-, -ifer-, -olog-, past participles in -ite; -ia/-eria = English -y/-ery stressed on i; remaining deviations are marked word by word in the Interlingua-English Dictionary. Coded here as right-edge, final-consonant-conditioned (final if C-final else penult) with lexical exceptions; a catalog may prefer 'fixed: other position/segment-conditioned'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the text speaks only of 'main stress'. Sec. 12 leaves intonation and sound duration to native habits.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult classes (-le/-ne/-re after vowel; -ic, -ica, -ico, -ide, -ido, -ula, -ulo; -issim-, -esim-, -ifer-, -olog-; participles in -ite per footnote to sec. 148); -ific/-ifico stressed on first i; -ia/-eria on i; dictionary-marked deviations e.g. abbatia (-ía), formica (-íca), thermometro (-ó-) (IED p. liii); sec. 11 explicitly tolerates variation such as kilómetro ~ kilométro; construe, procrea, diminue, substitue follow the standard rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Prescriptive norm for a constructed auxiliary language (word-level citation forms, no written accent marks per sec. 1); sec. 11 states stress regularity 'should not be exaggerated' and native habits may prevail, so realized stress varies by speaker background.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Interlingua of IALA (1951; ISO 639 ina, Glottolog inte1239), the naturalistic Romance-based auxiliary language codified by Gode; not Peano's Latino sine Flexione (also once called 'Interlingua') and not Occidental/Interlingue (ile). The rule is a prescriptive norm; sec. 11 of the same source concedes speaker variation.

sources.note: Ch. 'Spelling and Pronunciation', sec. 10 (p. 5): main stress normally on the vowel before the last consonant; plural ending does not move it; -le/-ne/-re after a vowel and suffixes -ic, -ica, -ico, -ide, -ido, -ula, -ulo give antepenult; vowel-only/CVV words like io, via stressed on first vowel; other deviations marked in the IED; sec. 11: stress regularity 'should not be exaggerated' (kilometro on 2nd or 3rd syllable both acceptable); sec. 1: no written accent marks. Footnote to sec. 148: past participles in -ite stressed on antepenult.

sources.note: Second-hand summary of Gode & Blair sec. 10: stress on the vowel before the last consonant, ignoring plural -(e)s; antepenult for -le/-ne/-re, -ica/-ico, -ide/-ido, -ula/-ulo; -ic penult; kilometro variable.
